content.intro: A web request carries a method, path, headers, and optional data; PHP uses these to produce a status, headers, and body. Keep HTTP details separate from application rules and templates. In this lesson, focus on $_get; then compare it with $_post. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use accessing request information when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A web request carries a method, path, headers, and optional data; PHP uses these to produce a status, headers, and body. Keep HTTP details separate from application rules and templates. For accessing request information, begin with $_get. Also distinguish $_post; $_server; $_request and its limitations. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
